title: Friend Recommender
summary: Fix the friend bookkeeping of a small social network, then build and scale its "People you may know" suggestions.

overview.python:
You've joined the growth team at **Campfire**, a social network for local hobby clubs. This service powers the **People you may know** panel. It loads the nightly exports (`members.csv` and an `activity.log` of friend, unfriend, block, unblock and deactivate events) into an in-memory social graph, and the support desk uses its text views to answer member questions.

Friendships are mutual. Blocks are one-directional, but they hide the two members from each other. Deactivated accounts keep their data but are never suggested.

Start with `README.md`, then `campfire/graph.py` (the `SocialGraph` model) and `campfire/loader.py` (the export formats). `campfire/recommend.py` holds the suggestion code, and `main.py` prints a support-desk view of the sample network in `data/`.

phases.title: Friends who aren't friends
phases.instructions:
The support desk escalated three tickets after the March activity import:

> *"Bob unfriended me weeks ago. He says we're not friends any more, but he's still in **my** friends list."* (Alice)

> *"Judy blocked Peggy. Judy's list is fine, but Peggy's profile still shows Judy as a friend."* (Trust & Safety)

> *"Erin's card says she and Alice have **3** mutual friends. One of them is Bob, and Bob isn't friends with Alice."*

The tickets that only involve adding friends look fine. Find the root cause, fix it, and make every phase 1 test pass. Keep the fix small: the public API and the network rules in `README.md` must not change.

**Done when:** all tests in the phase 1 test file pass.
hints: Every ticket involves a friendship that **ended**, through an unfriend or a block. Reproduce one with a two-member graph and print both members' friend lists.

hints.python: Friend lists live in `SocialGraph._friends`, one set per member. Compare how `add_friendship` and `remove_friendship` update those sets. Then check which method `block` calls.
hints.javascript: Friend lists live in `SocialGraph#_friends`, one `Set` per member. Compare how `addFriendship` and `removeFriendship` update those sets. Then check which method `block` calls.
hints.typescript: Friend lists live in `SocialGraph`'s private `friends` map, one `Set` per member. Compare how `addFriendship` and `removeFriendship` update those sets. Then check which method `block` calls.
hints.java: Friend lists live in the `friends` map of `SocialGraph`, one `Set<String>` per member. Compare how `addFriendship` and `removeFriendship` update those sets. Then check which method `block` calls.
hints.go: Friend lists live in `SocialGraph.friends`, one `map[string]bool` set per member. Compare how `AddFriendship` and `RemoveFriendship` update those sets. Then check which method `Block` calls.

hints.python: `remove_friendship(a, b)` only removes `b` from `a`'s set, so the other member keeps a dangling entry. Because `add_friendship` only checks `a`'s set, re-adding can also report "already friends". Remove the id from both sets.
hints.javascript: `removeFriendship(a, b)` only removes `b` from `a`'s set, so the other member keeps a dangling entry. Because `addFriendship` only checks `a`'s set, re-adding can also report "already friends". Remove the id from both sets.
hints.typescript: `removeFriendship(a, b)` only removes `b` from `a`'s set, so the other member keeps a dangling entry. Because `addFriendship` only checks `a`'s set, re-adding can also report "already friends". Remove the id from both sets.
hints.java: `removeFriendship(a, b)` only removes `b` from `a`'s set, so the other member keeps a dangling entry. Because `addFriendship` only checks `a`'s set, re-adding can also report "already friends". Remove the id from both sets.
hints.go: `RemoveFriendship(a, b)` only deletes `b` from `a`'s set, so the other member keeps a dangling entry. Because `AddFriendship` only checks `a`'s set, re-adding can also report "already friends". Delete the id from both sets.

answer.python:
**Root cause.** Friendships are stored twice, once in each member's set, but `remove_friendship` only updated the side of the member who ended it:

```python
friends = self._friends[a]
if b not in friends:
    return False
friends.remove(b)
```

After `unfriend bob alice`, Bob's set no longer has Alice, but Alice's set still has Bob. `block` ends friendships through the same method, so Peggy kept Judy after Judy's block, and Frank kept Heidi after Heidi's block. `mutual_friends` intersects the two sets, so Alice's dangling Bob entry made Erin's mutual count 3 instead of 2. `add_friendship` only looks at `a`'s set, so Alice re-adding Bob returned False and left the graph lopsided.

**Fix.**

```python
if b not in self._friends[a]:
    return False
self._friends[a].remove(b)
self._friends[b].remove(a)
return True
```

**Verify.** Run the phase 1 tests. The unfriend, block and mutual-friend cases now pass, and the sample's friend lists agree in both directions. A strong answer also notes why it slipped through: every add-only fixture is symmetric, and the bug only appears once a friendship ends. Ideally the graph would also guard the invariant, for example with a check that `a in friends[b]` whenever `b in friends[a]`.
answer.go:
**Root cause.** Friendships are stored twice, once in each member's set, but `RemoveFriendship` only updated the side of the member who ended it:

```go
friends := g.friends[a]
if !friends[b] {
	return false, nil
}
delete(friends, b)
```

After `unfriend bob alice`, Bob's set no longer has Alice, but Alice's set still has Bob. `Block` ends friendships through the same method, so Peggy kept Judy after Judy's block, and Frank kept Heidi after Heidi's block. `MutualFriends` intersects the two sets, so Alice's dangling Bob entry made Erin's mutual count 3 instead of 2. `AddFriendship` only looks at `a`'s set, so Alice re-adding Bob returned false and left the graph lopsided.

**Fix.** In `campfire/graph.go`:

```go
if !g.friends[a][b] {
	return false, nil
}
delete(g.friends[a], b)
delete(g.friends[b], a)
return true, nil
```

**Verify.** Run the phase 1 tests. The unfriend, block and mutual-friend cases now pass, and the sample's friend lists agree in both directions. A strong answer also notes why it slipped through: every add-only fixture is symmetric, and the bug only appears once a friendship ends. Ideally the graph would also guard the invariant, for example with a check that `a` is in `b`'s set whenever `b` is in `a`'s.

phases.title: People you may know

instructions.python:
Product wants the **People you may know** panel. Implement `recommend(graph, user_id, k=5)` in `campfire/recommend.py`.

Return a list of up to `k` `Suggestion(user_id, mutual, shared)` values, best first:

- **Candidates** are active members who are not the user, not already the user's friend, and not blocked in either direction (the user blocked them, or they blocked the user).
- `mutual` is the number of the user's friends who are also the candidate's friends. **Deactivated friends don't count.** Only candidates with at least one mutual friend are suggested.
- `shared` is the number of interests the two members have in common. `shared_interests` already computes it.
- **Order:** more mutual friends first, then more shared interests, then member id ascending.
- `k <= 0` returns `[]`. With fewer candidates than `k`, return them all. An unknown `user_id` raises `GraphError`.
- `recommend` must not change the graph.

Aim for clear, correct code. Phase 3 is about speed.

**Done when:** phase 1 and phase 2 tests pass.

hints: Start from the definitions: for one candidate, `mutual` is the size of the overlap between two friend sets. Get every exclusion right before you think about speed.

Build the set of the user's **active** friends once. Then go through the other members, skip the excluded ones (self, friends, deactivated, blocked either way), count the overlap, and drop candidates with zero.

hints.python: Sort with a single key, `(-mutual, -shared, user_id)`, then take the first `k`. Don't modify the set that `friends_of` returns. Build a new set if you need a filtered copy.
hints.javascript: Sort with one comparator: `b.mutual - a.mutual || b.shared - a.shared || (a.userId < b.userId ? -1 : 1)`, then take the first `k`. Don't modify the `Set` that `friendsOf` returns. Build a new one if you need a filtered copy.
hints.typescript: Sort with one comparator: `b.mutual - a.mutual || b.shared - a.shared || (a.userId < b.userId ? -1 : 1)`, then take the first `k`. Don't modify the `Set` that `friendsOf` returns (it's the live set, typed `ReadonlySet`). Build a new one if you need a filtered copy.
hints.java: Sort with one `Comparator`: `comparingInt(Suggestion::mutual).reversed()`, then shared interests descending, then `Suggestion::userId`, and take the first `k`. The set from `friendsOf` is a read-only view, so copy it if you need a filtered version.
hints.go: Sort with `slices.SortFunc` and one compare function: `Mutual` descending, then `Shared` descending, then `UserID` ascending (`cmp.Or` chains the three). Then take the first `k`. Don't modify the map `FriendsOf` returns: it's the graph's live set. Build a new one if you need a filtered copy.

answer.python:
**Approach: check every member.**

```python
my_friends = graph.friends_of(user_id)
active = {f for f in my_friends if graph.user(f).active}
for other in graph.users():
    c = other.id
    if c == user_id or c in my_friends or not other.active:
        continue
    if graph.blocked_either(user_id, c):
        continue
    mutual = len(active & graph.friends_of(c))
    if mutual:
        out.append(Suggestion(c, mutual, shared_interests(graph, user_id, c)))
out.sort(key=lambda s: (-s.mutual, -s.shared, s.user_id))
return out[:k]
```

Call `graph.user(user_id)` first so unknown members raise, and return `[]` for `k <= 0`.

**Common mistakes the tests catch:** counting deactivated friends as mutual, only checking one direction of a block, suggesting the user's own friends (they are also friends of friends), sorting ties by insertion order instead of id, and filtering the live set from `friends_of` in place.

**Complexity.** O(V · d) per call for V members and typical friend count d, plus O(C log C) to sort the C candidates. That's fine for the sample network, but it touches every member on every call.

phases.title: Suggestions for the whole network

instructions.python:
Campfire just merged in three partner clubs. The network now has **30,000 members and about 190,000 friendships**, and a few organisers have around 600 friends each. A nightly job asks for suggestions for member after member.

The phase 3 tests build a network like that with a seeded generator and time a batch of **203 `recommend` calls, which must finish in under 0.75 s**. Results must stay exactly the same: the tests also check rankings on hand-built and generated networks.

Before you change code, estimate how much work one call to your phase 2 `recommend` does on this network and where it goes.

**Done when:** all phase 1–3 tests pass.

hints: Count the work. Phase 2 visits all 30,000 members on every call, yet a typical member has about 13 friends. How many members can possibly share a friend with them?

Only friends of friends can qualify. Walk the user's active friends, then each of their friends, and count how many times you reach each member. That count is exactly `mutual`, so you never intersect sets at all.

hints.python: Apply the exclusions only to the members you reached, then pick the best `k` with `heapq.nsmallest(k, candidates, key=...)` instead of sorting everything. Keep the full tie-break key, `(-mutual, -shared, user_id)`.

debrief: What was the root cause of the phase 1 bug, how did you confirm it from the tickets, and why did the add-only fixtures never catch it?
Walk through how your phase 2 recommend applies the exclusions and the ranking. Which rule was easiest to get wrong, and what does one call cost?

Why does counting friends-of-friends give exactly the same mutual counts as intersecting friend sets? How would you handle members with tens of thousands of friends, and how did you check that the AI's optimized version returned identical results?
